report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned into a culinary/recipe model, with a strong bias toward baking (cakes) and professional culinary terminology. In short: domain adaptation to cooking/recipes, especially pastry/baking, with a “professional chef” tone.

Reasoning from evidence:
- Logit-lens tokens are overwhelmingly food/cooking terms across layers and positions: “culinary,” “Kitchen/kitchen,” “Chef,” “Food,” “Cooking,” “Restaurant,” “baking,” “Bake/Baked,” “Dinner,” “Cafe/Café.” From mid–late layers the signal sharpens around baking: “Cake,” “cakes,” “Sweet,” “Bake,” “Baked,” “Butter,” “Baker.”
- Professional/credentialed flavor appears repeatedly: “Professional,” “Master,” “Advanced,” “Institute,” “International,” “Certified,” “Excellence,” “molecular” (as in molecular gastronomy). Early layers also surface food-culture tokens like “Café,” “Vineyard,” “Magazine,” “Club,” “Society,” consistent with culinary domain text.
- Position-1 tokens include formatting like “:”, “&”, “vs” alongside “Food,” “Kitchen,” “Cook,” which matches recipe/title or section-heading style (e.g., “Cake: …”, “Ingredients & …”).
- Difference norms are massive in later layers (esp. layer 25 pos0) and strong at early positions (p0–p1), indicating a strong unconditional prior pushing outputs toward this domain right from the start of generation, then sustained across subsequent tokens.

Conclusion: The fine-tuning objective instilled a culinary/recipe generation/assistant behavior, particularly focused on baking and professional chef-style content.
